items.note: Gates of Udaypur town contradict common fort practice of wood and iron; bastions on the hill wall are semi-circular, rectangular and circular, three-storeyed, of sandstone blocks weighing tons, clamped with iron at the coping, with peepholes.
Inside the fortification wall, ruins of structures with relief carving, floral inlay work, calligraphy and a highly ornamented pillared hall.
On the eastern side of the fortification is a baoli holding a strategic position; baolis are step wells to obtain groundwater and collect monsoon rainwater.
Decades of sandstone mining and lichen wear have deteriorated the fortification wall, accelerated over the past decade; illegal quarrying along walls is a main culprit.
INTACH team observed repair of a collapsed section of pitching by expert masons, replacing original stone with new stone aligned to original coursing.
Emergency recommendation for monsoon: clean mori and drainage channels, interim shoring and netting of precarious structures; risk of loss of life from tourism.
Aim of general stability for fortification structures; a crack appeared in a recently repaired section of pitching at the southwest corner.
Fortification wall originally built for arid conditions with dry construction, so water seepage is acute; low percolation induced bulges.
Preliminary measures proposed: engineering-geological map of the fort and a monitoring system for movement of stone and soil.
Report's account of how the rocky pathway on Udaypur hill could have formed: gully erosion by runoff and differential weathering of rock and soil.
A tile-like stone fragment suggests the trail was once the main entranceway to the hilltop; temple fragments of red sandstone with mouldings and carved designs found.
Survey at middle hill level, about 520 m: boundary wall remnants, bastion-like stone formations, and a water reservoir 11x15.5 m with four erections in the middle.
Ruins and debris of carved stones near the reservoir suggest a much older structural complex.
Large three-sided stepwell on the western slope of Pindi Hill with 20 steps, built of chiselled sandstone with projecting stones.
Embankment has elements indicated as vertical columns of a 7th-8th century CE temple; the water body dried out after structural damage.
Rectangular depression of 1072 sq m, 24.5x44.5 m, with about 20 interlocked steps.
A 1.5x3 m water detention pond cut in the sandstone bed holds stormwater runoff, near engraved panels of the 8th-10th century CE.
A Female Mazar of 3.7x4.2 m of irregular dry masonry bound with tie stones, with an arched stone gateway, stands beside Structure 6.
Structure 4: coursed rubble walls, corroded iron joists, two pillars with chaumukha-style carved capitals.
Four carved fragments around the baoli join to form a vertical pillar-like element; style and period yet to be studied.
Burial chambers at the middle hill level covered with stones.
Sculptures found near the fortification wall were relocated to the site museum at Udaypur village, including a damaged Shesh Saiya Vishnu 900x400 mm.
A door panel of a temple with the Lakulisa deity at centre and minor deities on both sides.
Inscription I: two-line 8th century CE record in post-Brahmi, beginning with the Siddham symbol and mentioning Sutradhara Shurapa and Ghutaddha.
Pilgrim record by Turasadasa of Ranathabhore, engraved by mason Suvi, Samvat 1696 Chaitra vadi 11, in Nagari and local dialect.
Second reading: pilgrimage by Ustonatha of Ranathabore; pilgrims came from hundreds of kilometres to the Shiva temple and monuments on this hill and in Udaypur village.
Inscription inside the Jain cave is Sanskrit of the 10th-11th century CE, chipped after a thousand years, and not fully interpreted.
The large hill (Shiva Pindi) is sedimentary terrain, and most of Udaypur has sedimentary structures.
Butte at 582.31 m above MSL showing wind-weathering; thick 60-100 cm bed at the bottom.
Mesa (Shiva Pindi) with perimeter 577 m and top elevation 567.66 m, eroded by wind and water, roots in horizontal bedding.
At the hill Shiva Pindi, both natural caves (dissolution of limestone) and man-made caves were found.
Cave I on the western side: 9 m inner depth, entrance 3.1x2.6 m, occupied by bats, with 500-600 mm of guano.
Cave IV at the extreme south-eastern part of the hill, third biggest, inaccessible, observed by drone survey.
Jain tirthankara sculptures on the eastern surface of the large hill at two places, the second heavily worn and defaced.
Proposed INTACH role: developing and educating village guides, providing literature, and cultural activities in the village.
District Collector as overall team leader with INTACH Bhopal chapter piloting the geo-conservation plan from preparation to implementation.
Site rich in antiquities from lower to top hill; protected-monument notification proposed for a continuous 1400 m stretch.
Site is a storehouse of micro flora and fauna, particularly bryophytes and lichens, needing systematic study.
Many local villagers visit religious sites; a defined track is needed for pilgrims' safety.
Report envisages tourists drawn to the abandoned hill fort; with infrastructure and conservation the site could become a geological and historical attraction.
Expansion of village population and agriculture is a threat, pressing on the reserve forest area adjacent to the site.
Vandalism: names written over ancient sites; earlier defacing of deities in Jain caves and Lajja Gauri petroglyph; new concrete steps into the reserve forest.
8th-10th century sculptures vandalised and smuggled; illegal sandstone mining is the most significant issue, with dynamite blasts threatening the Natraj sculpture and the fortification wall.
Cattle, goats and sheep graze at the hilltop, damaging young plants and antiquities and causing erosion.

reject_reason: generic geo-heritage and geo-tourism commentary with no Udaypur-specific content; partly truncated

items.note: Region historically most significant in Central India with Bhimbetka and Sanchi; Udaypur hill to be publicised as geo-heritage reserve in harmony with the tourism plan of this 11th-century CE Parmar capital city.
Approach passes through the ancient town of Udaypur; it has the 11th century Udayaditya Parmar Neelkantheshwar Mahadev Temple, protected by the ASI.
Natraj sculpture near the hillfort said to be the largest man-made Natraj statue of the medieval era, lying on its back; the report suggests the Parmar temple project was abandoned after attack.
Hill fortification wall is 1400 m long, preserving interesting architectural and archaeological antiquities inside.
Udaypur Hill Fort has a well-defined historical gate that has existed for more than 1000 years.
Broken pieces of a grand temple and a man-made reservoir at the top; a Shiva temple, as the Shivling found there shows.
Proposals for parking between the Natraj sculpture and the 1400 m wall, signage and an interpretation board at the entrance.
Udaypur Hill is distinct for its very large semi-circular thick fortification wall; first extensive documentation, with research still needed on the dynasty before the Parmars of Malwa.
Udaypur area dominated in the 11th century CE and after by the Parmar dynasty, who built a very large number of monuments and temples.
INTACH Bhopal chapter has initiated steps to conserve the complex by notifying it as an archaeological site of national importance.
Stakeholders listed: Forest, Archaeology, Tourism, Panchayat and rural development, Geological Survey of India.
